category_title: Young immigrant boys labeled as 'struggling readers' who exhibit non-normative behavioral engagement (e.g., movement, talk, and gaze aversion) during literacy tasks
minimal_context: The student is sitting on the rug with a group for a read-aloud of the book 'Visiting Day'.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Alright everyone, please sit in your designated spots on the rug. Today we are going to do a read-aloud of the book 'Visiting Day'.

STUDENT: (Looking at another student instead of sitting in his spot) Ooh, ooh! I knew it! The father is in jail and little girl’s visiting her father.

TUTOR: Please remember our rules for the rug. You need to sit quietly in your spot and not talk out of turn.

STUDENT: But you know, there are so many rules to remember that I can’t remember what I was gonna say sometimes.

TUTOR: We just need to sit still and be quiet so I can start reading the story to the group.

STUDENT: (Sighs heavily) I’ve already heard it four times! (Slumps over, turns his back away, and averts his gaze)

options.A: Show the student the book and ask if he would like to take it home to draw a picture of it, then bring it back.
options.B: Ask a follow-up question that links the student's physical sensation on the rug to a potential emotional state.
options.C: Make expectations clear while respectfully letting the student know that the tutor wants to hear what he has to say.
options.D: Remind the children on the rug that reading also involves listening—to the reader and to each other.
